sections.skill: Compute markup and margin and tell them apart

questions.prompt: Cost 5 dollars, price 8 dollars. What is the markup?
questions.intro: MARKUP and MARGIN both describe the gap between cost and price, but they use different bases. MARKUP is the gap as a percent of COST: (price - cost) / cost. MARGIN is the gap as a percent of PRICE: (price - cost) / price. Example: cost 6 dollars, price 10 dollars. The gap is 4. Markup = 4 / 6, about 67 percent. Margin = 4 / 10 = 40 percent. Markup is always bigger than margin for the same item. Mixing them up can lead to prices that are too low.

sections.skill: Writing a part as a percent of a whole

questions.prompt: What percent is 2 of 8?
questions.intro: To find what percent one number is of another, divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100. Example: 3 out of 12 is 3 / 12 = 0.25 = 25 percent. The number you divide BY is the base. Changing the base changes the answer: 3 / 4 = 75 percent, but 3 / 12 = 25 percent. Always ask, "percent OF what?"

sections.skill: Markup looks back at cost; margin looks at the price tag

questions.prompt: Markup compares the gap with what?
questions.intro: Picture a price tag of 10 dollars on an item that cost 6 dollars. Markup asks, "How much did I add compared with what I paid?" (4 compared with 6). Margin asks, "How much of the price tag do I keep?" (4 out of 10). Same 4 dollars, different comparison. Remember: Markup looks at what you paid; Margin looks at the price tag.
